item.title: Fixing Date/Time Parsing Issues: Format M vs m and Year 'u' vs 'y'
item.description:
“Fixing Date/Time Parsing Issues: Format M vs m and Year ‘u’ vs ‘y’”

When working with date and time manipulation in modern Java or Kotlin, correctly specifying the pattern in DateTimeFormatter is critical. Several common pitfalls involve confusing month and minute placeholders, or selecting the appropriate year representation. How does one correctly handle parsing ISO standard date-time strings and formatting them while avoiding common pattern mismatches?

Why Does My Date/Time String Parse Without an Explicit Formatter?

For an input string conforming precisely to the ISO 8601 standard, such as "2006-03-25T10:30:00+12:00", the default parsing mechanism, specifically OffsetDateTime#parse(), often succeeds without supplying an explicit DateTimeFormatter.

item.title: Parsing ISO 8601 Timestamps in Java: Dealing with 'T' and 'Z' Separators
item.description:
“Parsing ISO 8601 Timestamps in Java: Dealing with ‘T’ and ‘Z’ Separators”

The format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss.SSSZ is a common representation defined by ISO 8601 . The central ‘T’ acts purely as a literal separator between the date and time elements, while the trailing ‘Z’ signifies a time zone offset of zero hours, commonly referred to as “Zulu time” or UTC.

Employing the Modern java.time API (Java 8+)

The java.time framework introduced in Java 8 is the preferred mechanism for handling date and time operations, superseding older, problematic classes like java.util.Date and SimpleDateFormat. These modern classes inherently favor ISO 8601 representations.

item.title: Robust Java Approaches for Calculating Age from Dates
item.description:
“Robust Java Approaches for Calculating Age from Dates”

How does one precisely determine a person’s age in years using Java, given various date inputs and libraries? Navigating date and time calculations in Java often involves choosing between legacy classes (java.util.Date, Calendar) and the superior, modern java.time API introduced in Java 8. Several viable strategies exist, each with its own trade-offs regarding simplicity, accuracy, and reliance on external dependencies.
